routines.name: _id_list
routines.docstring:
Validate an optional list of nonempty change-ID strings.

Applied to both `depends_on` and `applied` because SPEC line 12 maps every
malformed dependency/journal shape to `invalid-change`; a bare string is
rejected rather than iterated so `"ab"` cannot silently become `a`,`b`.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate records and collapse identical duplicates.

Rows share an identity iff id, component, units and the dependency *set*
are all equal (SPEC line 11), so dependency order in the input carries no
meaning and is normalized to a sorted tuple. Output is sorted by ID; that
is for stability only - planner rebuilds execution order from the graph.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Validate the persisted applied journal injected by the caller.

Duplicates collapse because replay is a set-membership question. Whether
an ID actually exists is a graph question, so it is answered in planner.

routines.name: _order
routines.docstring:
Return the full deterministic topological order of every change ID.

Among currently eligible changes the smallest ID is taken first, which is
what makes the order reproducible across runs and inputs (SPEC line 13).
Missing targets and cycles are structural faults: no partial order is
returned, because a partial release is worse than a refused one.

comments: # Anything left over sits on a cycle; report it instead of silently
# dropping those changes from the action list.
# The caller's journal claims a release this request cannot see;
# treating it as applied would silently skip unknown history.
# Reverse of the *full* order, then filtered: applied changes come down
# in exact reverse dependency order even if part of the graph is not
# applied. Budget is validated by policy but must not cap a rollback.
# Already-applied entries satisfy dependencies (they precede their
# dependents in `order`) and cost nothing now: they are skipped before
# the budget check so replayed journal entries cannot exhaust it.

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
Validate the G2 `retain` hint: a defaulted, duplicate-free ID list.

Only `rollback` reads it (CHANGE-G2.md line 7); calendar `plan` callers
that send it anyway must not be rejected or influenced, so this check is
invoked from the rollback branch only.

Shape faults map to `invalid-retain`, not `invalid-change`, so the caller
can tell a broken journal/dependency from a broken retention request. The
separate error code is also why `_id_list` is not reused directly here:
every shape rule is restated so the code stays `invalid-retain`. Whether
each ID is applied is answered by the planner after applied validation,
never here, because that needs the deduplicated journal and graph.

# caller's data, not a merge opportunity: fail closed instead of
# guessing which record wins.
# A bare string is rejected instead of iterated: iterating would silently
# reinterpret it as separate IDs.
# Duplicates are rejected rather than collapsed: a repeated ID in a
# retention request is ambiguous about the caller's intent, so fail
# closed instead of guessing.

routines.name: _retained_set
routines.docstring:
Expand a validated `retain` request into the applied IDs to keep.

Called only for rollback and only after the graph and journal passed, so
the adjacency built here is known acyclic and every ID it sees names a real
change. Retention is a *safety* claim: "this release stays up", so anything
it transitively depends on must stay up too - rolling a dependency out from
under a kept service would break the promise the field exists to make.

Only applied nodes enter the closure: a dependency that was never applied
is neither emitted nor kept, so it never appears in the result either way.

comments: # Anything left over sits on a cycle; report it instead of silently
# dropping those changes from the action list.
# Deliberately checked here rather than in journal: "is it applied"
# needs the validated journal, so raising earlier would mask
# unknown-dependency and dependency-cycle faults in the same request.
# Dependencies of each change, taken from the already-validated records.
# Walking *down* dependents would be the wrong closure: it would keep
# services that merely depend on a kept one, whereas keeping a service
# requires keeping what it needs to run.
# Walk up the depends_on edges from each retained ID, so every applied
# dependency (transitively) is kept too. The graph is acyclic - `_order`
# already refused cycles before this runs - and `keep` guards re-entry, so
# this terminates even on deep chains.
# The order here is contract, not accident: transport happens in
# release.py, then structural request/change faults, then policy
# (budget/environment/action, which raises production-frozen), then graph
# faults, then rollback-only retain checks, then the quota. A caller fixes
# the earliest problem and sees the next; a frozen or malformed request is
# never reported as merely over budget.
# The caller's journal claims a release this request cannot see;
# treating it as applied would silently skip unknown history.
# Reverse of the *full* order, then filtered: applied changes come down
# in exact reverse dependency order even if part of the graph is not
# applied. Budget is validated by policy but must not cap a rollback.
# Kept changes are omitted rather than emitted, so they cost no units
# and no partial action is ever produced for them.
# Already-applied entries satisfy dependencies (they precede their
# dependents in `order`) and cost nothing now: they are skipped before
# the budget check so replayed journal entries cannot exhaust it.
# `retain` is rollback-only: a plan carrying it is ignored, not
# rejected, so one request shape can be reused across actions.
# G2 quota (CHANGE-G2.md line 6): the effective allowance is the smaller of
# the caller's budget and the staging ceiling, so asking for more cannot
# widen it. Rollback stays uncapped on purpose - a cap there would strand a
# release half-reverted.

routines.name: _member

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Return (budget, action) after validating the policy fields.

Raises `production-frozen` for production once `environment`, `action` and

only a staging `plan` uses it as a cap: rollback must undo whatever is
applied, so a cap would strand a release in a half-reverted state.
`type(...) is int` keeps JSON `true`/`false` out. Planner applies
STAGING_PLAN_LIMIT on top of the returned budget; nothing is clamped here.

comments: # G1 authorized both actions in both environments (SPEC line 14); G2 freezes
# production (CHANGE-G2.md line 5), so this set now only describes what staging
# may run. Widening it is the single place that changes authorization, so
# planner never duplicates the decision.
# G2 effective staging plan budget (CHANGE-G2.md line 6). Policy owns the number
# so the quota has exactly one definition; planner only compares against it and
# never clamps the caller's value itself.
# G2 freeze, deliberately after the request-shape and budget checks so a
# malformed environment/action/budget still reports its own error, but
# before any graph or change inspection (CHANGE-G2.md line 5): production

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate and normalize the ``changes`` array.

Returns records in input order with ``depends_on`` as a list of strings.
Duplicate handling is intentionally NOT done here: ``read_request`` needs
every raw record in order to tell equality from conflict.

routines.name: collapse
routines.docstring:
Collapse identical duplicate records; return ``{id: record}``.

Identity for equality is id + component + units + the *set* of
dependencies: input order inside ``depends_on`` is not semantic, so
``["b","a"]`` and ``["a","b"]`` are the same record. Two records with the
same id but a different signature are ``conflicting-change``.

Why collapse before accounting: the planner charges the budget per emitted
action, and a change listed twice is still one action. Deduping later would
either double-charge or make the result depend on which copy won.

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Return the full deterministic topological order of ``changes``.

``changes`` is the collapsed ``{id: record}`` map. ``applied`` is the
validated set of persisted change IDs; it is checked for membership here
but otherwise does not affect ordering (an applied change is still a node
in the graph, it is just not emitted by ``plan``).

Ordering rule: at every step choose the lexicographically smallest ID among
*currently eligible* changes (all dependencies already placed). A heap is
used so that ties never depend on input order or on dict iteration order.

Cycle detection is over the whole graph, including nodes that are already
applied. A cycle among applied changes still makes the graph
inconsistent -- and would also make the reverse rollback order
ill-defined -- so it is rejected even though no action is emitted from it.

routines.name: read_request
routines.docstring:
Validate ``changes`` + persisted ``applied`` and build the plan state.

Returns ``(order, by_id, applied_ids)`` where ``order`` is the full
deterministic topological order and ``by_id`` the collapsed records.

comments: # ``type(...) is int`` rather than isinstance: JSON true/false decode to
# bool, and bool is a subclass of int, so isinstance(True, int) is True.
# The spec says integers exclude booleans.
# Keep the first occurrence as the canonical copy (input-order
# stable; the copies are equal by definition anyway).
# else: identical duplicate, silently reduced to one record.
# The caller claims to have applied something we were never told
# about: the release journal and the change list disagree.
# ``set`` collapses repeated entries in one ``depends_on``; otherwise
# ["b","b"] would count b twice and never reach in-degree zero.
# Self-dependency is a one-element cycle and must NOT be filtered
# out; it falls through to the cycle branch below.
journal.py.moduleNote:
Normalize release records at the input boundary and rebuild release state.

This module owns three things that must agree with each other:

* record shape / identity (``invalid-change``, ``conflicting-change``),
* the caller-supplied persisted ``applied`` journal
  (``invalid-change``, ``unknown-dependency``),
* the dependency graph and its deterministic topological order
  (``unknown-dependency``, ``dependency-cycle``).

It never looks at ``environment``, ``action`` or ``budget``; that is policy's
job, and policy runs first in ``planner.plan``.

comments: # Reverse the FULL order, then keep the applied ones. Reversing the
# filtered subsequence would usually give the same answer, but building
# from the full order is the guarantee: a change is undone only after
# everything that depends on it, applied or not.
# ``order`` is already topological and dependency-satisfying because
# applied entries are part of the graph, they are just not emitted.
# Charge emitted units only: applied entries cost nothing and duplicates
# were already collapsed, so this equals "units after replay/dedup".
# Rollback validates the budget in policy but is never capped by it.
planner.py.moduleNote: Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

routines.name: check
routines.docstring:
Return ``{"budget": int, "action": str, "environment": str}``.

Rejection order is environment -> action -> budget. It matches the G0/G1
baseline: a request with an unknown environment and an unknown action still
reports ``invalid-environment``.

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring: Backward-compatible accessor kept for callers of the G0 API.

comments: # G1: every environment supports both actions. G2 (see CHANGE-G2.md) is the
# place to narrow this down, e.g. by environment.
# ``type(...) is int`` excludes JSON booleans (bool is a subclass of int).
policy.py.moduleNote:
Validate release policy before computing actions.

Policy is the gate: it decides whether the request may run at all and how many
units it may emit. It intentionally never looks at ``changes`` -- record
validation belongs to journal, and the gate must be answerable without building
the graph.

``check`` returns a context dict instead of a bare budget so the planner can
tell "this is a rollback" from "this is a plan" without re-deriving policy.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate and normalize the ``changes`` array.

Returns records in input order with ``depends_on`` as a list of strings.
Duplicate handling is intentionally NOT done here: ``read_request`` needs
every raw record in order to tell equality from conflict.

G2 #1 note: production is rejected by ``policy.check_frozen`` before the
planner calls this function, so ``invalid-change`` is never reported for a
frozen environment even when the records are malformed. That ordering is
the requirement, not an accident of call order.

routines.name: collapse
routines.docstring:
Collapse identical duplicate records; return ``{id: record}``.

Identity for equality is id + component + units + the *set* of
dependencies: input order inside ``depends_on`` is not semantic, so
``["b","a"]`` and ``["a","b"]`` are the same record. Two records with the
same id but a different signature are ``conflicting-change``.

Why collapse before accounting: the planner charges the budget per emitted
action, and a change listed twice is still one action. Deduping later would
either double-charge or make the result depend on which copy won.

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Return the full deterministic topological order of ``changes``.

``changes`` is the collapsed ``{id: record}`` map. ``applied`` is the
validated set of persisted change IDs; it is checked for membership here
but otherwise does not affect ordering (an applied change is still a node
in the graph, it is just not emitted by ``plan``).

Ordering rule: at every step choose the lexicographically smallest ID among
*currently eligible* changes (all dependencies already placed). A heap is
used so that ties never depend on input order or on dict iteration order.

Cycle detection is over the whole graph, including nodes that are already
applied. A cycle among applied changes still makes the graph
inconsistent -- and would also make the reverse rollback order
ill-defined -- so it is rejected even though no action is emitted from it.

G2 subtlety: this order is *independent of the environment's frozen state*.
The planner calls ``policy.check_frozen`` before it ever gets here, so a
frozen production request never reaches this function. Do not move cycle
detection ahead of the freeze to "fail faster": G2 #1 explicitly requires a
malformed graph in production to still report ``production-frozen``.
Equally, ``retain`` (G2 #3) does not change this order; it only filters the
reversed order afterwards (see ``planner.plan``).

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
G2 #3: validate the rollback ``retain`` list.

``retain`` defaults to empty; when present it must be an array of change
IDs (non-empty strings, same shape rule as ``depends_on`` entries). It is
returned as a ``set`` so repeated IDs are harmless. Rejection here is pure
shape: "is this ID actually applied?" needs the journal and is checked in
``retained_ids``.

routines.name: _dependencies
routines.docstring: ``{id: set(dep, ...)}``; repeated entries collapse, self-edges are kept.

routines.name: retained_ids
routines.docstring:
The applied IDs that must stay: ``retain`` plus its applied dependencies.

``retain`` is closed over the dependency relation transitively, so a kept
change never loses a dependency it needs at runtime. Only IDs that are both
in the closure *and* in ``applied_ids`` are returned: a dependency that was
never applied is not in the database, so there is nothing to retain, and
the release still satisfies the graph.

Anything in ``retain`` that is not applied is ``invalid-retain`` -- asking
to keep something the journal says was never installed is a caller bug, and
silently ignoring it would make the rollback plan differ from the request.

The dependency edges of applied-but-not-retained nodes are still walked:
an applied node reached *through* a non-retained node cannot happen (the
walk starts at ``retain``), but a retained node may depend on an applied
node that itself depends on the retained set. Walking only downward from
``retain`` covers both cases and terminates on the already-validated DAG.

routines.name: read_request
routines.docstring:
Validate ``changes`` + persisted ``applied`` and build the plan state.

Returns ``(order, by_id, applied_ids)`` where ``order`` is the full
deterministic topological order and ``by_id`` the collapsed records.

``retain`` is *not* read here: it is parsed by ``read_retain`` and applied
by ``retained_ids`` so that ``read_request`` stays the same call the plan
path uses. Keeping the replay/graph call identical for both actions means
a plan and a rollback of the same request always agree about the graph.

comments: # ``type(...) is int`` rather than isinstance: JSON true/false decode to
# bool, and bool is a subclass of int, so isinstance(True, int) is True.
# The spec says integers exclude booleans.
# Keep the first occurrence as the canonical copy (input-order
# stable; the copies are equal by definition anyway).
# else: identical duplicate, silently reduced to one record.
# The caller claims to have applied something we were never told
# about: the release journal and the change list disagree.
# ``set`` collapses repeated entries in one ``depends_on``; otherwise
# ["b","b"] would count b twice and never reach in-degree zero.
# Self-dependency is a one-element cycle and must NOT be filtered
# out; it falls through to the cycle branch below.
# Covers both "known but not applied" and "not in ``changes`` at
# all" (``topological_order`` already rejected unknown journal
# IDs, so the second case cannot reach here from ``plan``; it can
# from a direct call). Both are "nonapplied" per G2 #3.
# ``retained`` doubles as the visited set; a DAG would not revisit,
# but this keeps the walk O(nodes + edges) even if that changes.
journal.py.moduleNote:
Normalize release records at the input boundary and rebuild release state.

This module owns three things that must agree with each other:

* record shape / identity (``invalid-change``, ``conflicting-change``),
* the caller-supplied persisted ``applied`` journal
  (``invalid-change``, ``unknown-dependency``),
* the dependency graph and its deterministic topological order
  (``unknown-dependency``, ``dependency-cycle``).

It never looks at ``environment``, ``action`` or ``budget``; that is policy's
job, and policy runs first in ``planner.plan``.

comments: # The ONLY failure shape. Every error path funnels through here, so
# ``actions``/``units`` cannot be partially filled by a caller that forgot
# to clear them: there is no shared mutable result to leak. SPEC's
# "a disallowed operation emits no partial actions" is therefore structural
# -- nothing is emitted until ``selected`` is fully built, and any raise
# before that point discards it.
# Gate order is deliberate and is *not* "cheapest check first":
#   1. shape of the environment/action/budget
#   2. the environment freeze        <- G2 #1, before any record is read
#   3. records, replay journal, graph, ordering
#   4. retain (rollback only)
# A frozen release must answer ``production-frozen`` even when its graph
# is malformed, so the freeze sits between 1 and 3 and not after them.
# ``check`` deliberately does not include the freeze itself: a frozen
# production request with a bad budget must still say
# ``production-frozen``, which is only possible if the freeze is not
# queued behind the budget shape check.
# ``retain`` is only meaningful for rollback (G2 #3). For ``plan`` it
# is parsed anyway so that a malformed list is still rejected rather
# than silently ignored -- accepting garbage on one path and rejecting
# it on another is how contracts drift. It has no effect on the plan.
# Both error types are ``ValueError`` subclasses whose message *is* the
# contract code, so no lookup table can fall out of sync with them.
# Nothing is emitted on this path: no partial actions ever escape.
# ``invalid-retain`` needs the journal, so it cannot be raised by
# ``read_retain``; it is part of the same all-or-nothing outcome.
# Reverse the FULL order, then keep the applied ones. Reversing the
# filtered subsequence would usually give the same answer, but building
# from the full order is the guarantee: a change is undone only after
# everything that depends on it, applied or not. ``retain`` subsets are
# removed *after* reversing so the relative order of the remaining IDs
# is unchanged by retention (G2 #3: "other applied IDs in the original
# deterministic reverse order").
# ``order`` is already topological and dependency-satisfying because
# applied entries are part of the graph, they are just not emitted.
# Charge emitted units only: applied entries cost nothing and duplicates
# were already collapsed, so this equals "units after replay/dedup". The
# limit is policy's ``effective_budget`` (request budget capped at 3 for
# staging plans, unbounded for rollback) -- the planner never re-implements
# the cap, or the two places could disagree about G2 #2.
planner.py.moduleNote: Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

routines.name: check
routines.docstring:
Return the gate context for an allowed request.

Keys: ``budget`` (the request budget, validated), ``action``,
``environment``. The effective emission limit is *not* a key here on
purpose: ``effective_budget(context)`` computes it, so the raw request
budget and the capped one can never drift apart.

Rejection order is environment -> action -> budget (all in ``check``), and
only then is ``check_frozen`` consulted by the planner. The freeze comes
*after* the three shape checks, so a request that is structurally invalid
still reports its transport code -- there is nothing to decide about an
operation whose request was never readable.

routines.name: check_frozen
routines.docstring:
G2 #1: production is staging-only; both actions are frozen.

Called by the planner right after ``check`` and *before* ``journal`` reads
``changes``, so a malformed graph in a production request still reports
``production-frozen`` rather than a graph error, and no partial actions can
be assembled from a frozen request.

routines.name: effective_budget
routines.docstring: The number of units this request may emit, after G2's staging cap.

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring: Backward-compatible accessor kept for callers of the G0 API.

comments: # Every environment supports both actions as *shape* values. G2 (CHANGE-G2.md
# #1) freezes only the *environment*: ``production`` is rejected with
# ``production-frozen`` in ``check_frozen``. The action set stays
# ``{plan, rollback}`` on purpose -- narrowing it here would make a frozen
# production request with ``action: "nope"`` report ``unsupported-action``
# instead of ``production-frozen``, i.e. an unknown action would outrank the
# environment freeze.
# G2 #2: the staging plan budget is ``min(request budget, 3)``. The cap lives in
# policy because "how many units may be emitted" is policy's question; the
# planner only compares emitted units against ``effective_budget`` and never
# re-derives the cap. Rollback is never capped (SPEC line 14 still holds).
# ``type(...) is int`` excludes JSON booleans (bool is a subclass of int).
# Rollback validates the budget in ``check`` but is never capped; returning
# infinity keeps the planner's single ``units > limit`` comparison correct
# without a second branch on the action.
policy.py.moduleNote:
Validate release policy before computing actions.

Policy is the gate: it decides whether the request may run at all and how many
units it may emit. It intentionally never looks at ``changes`` -- record
validation belongs to journal, and the gate must be answerable without building
the graph.

``check`` returns a context dict instead of a bare budget so the planner can
tell "this is a rollback" from "this is a plan" without re-deriving policy.

comments: # Unreadable transport is the only thing release.py itself classifies;
# everything else is a domain decision made below. ``1e999`` and
# ``NaN`` arrive here too: json accepts them as float('inf')/nan, and
# the planner then rejects them as ``invalid-request`` (float, not int)
# -- so neither path can produce a non-JSON serialisation.
# Last-resort net, separate from the JSON catch above so a bug and
# a bad byte stream stay distinguishable in a trace. The contract
# says "always exit normally with a JSON result"; a bug must not
# turn into a traceback on stderr and an empty stdout, which a
# caller cannot distinguish from a crash. ``actions`` stay empty: a
# crash never emits partial work. This is a safety net, NOT a
# contract -- if it ever fires the suite is the only thing that
# will show the underlying bug, because the caller only sees
# ``invalid-request``.
# Compact separators keep the stdout line byte-stable for callers that
# diff or log it; the key order is the SPEC's, and dicts preserve it.
release.py.moduleNote: JSON transport for the release planner.

routines.name: _id_list
routines.docstring: Validate an array of nonempty change IDs, deduplicated in first-seen order.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate change records; identical duplicates collapse to one.

A malformed record fails outright. An otherwise valid record also fails

routines.name: _dependencies
routines.docstring:
Return the dependency list of one raw record, normalized to a tuple.

`depends_on` defaults to an empty array. A missing key and an explicit
`null` are both rejected as invalid-change because SPEC only sanctions the
absent-key default: silently treating null/false/0 as "no dependencies"
would let a malformed caller erase edges from the graph.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate and normalize the `changes` array.

Returns a list of dicts with exact keys id/component/units/depends_on,
where `depends_on` is a de-duplicated tuple of dependency IDs.

Records are NOT deduplicated here; callers get `dedupe_changes` so that
validation of the whole input completes before any identity reasoning,
which keeps the error-code ordering deterministic (invalid-change beats
conflicting-change).

routines.name: dedupe_changes
routines.docstring:
Collapse identical records, reject conflicting reuse of an ID.

Equality "covers id, component, units and the set of dependencies": the
same edges listed in a different order are the same record, so we compare
`frozenset(depends_on)`. Any difference for the same id (including a
different dependency order only if it also changes the set) is a conflict,
because picking one of the two silently would make replay non-deterministic.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Validate the persisted release journal of applied change IDs.

Missing -> empty (caller may omit it). Non-array or non-string/empty
entries -> invalid-change. Duplicates collapse: the journal is a set of
facts, and emitting one action twice (or counting it twice) would violate
the "identical duplicates collapse" rule on the input side too.

routines.name: validate_applied
routines.docstring:
Every applied ID must exist in the request's change set.

Reporting unknown-dependency (rather than ignoring the stray entry) is a
replay safeguard: a caller whose journal references a record we cannot see
has a diverged journal, and acting on that state could emit a release from
an inconsistent baseline.

comments: # A self-edge is a one-node cycle; leaving it in would make the node
# never become eligible, but the cycle error would be emitted late and
# with worse diagnostics, so it is simply handled by cycle detection.
# Heap, not sorted(list) per step: among all currently eligible changes we
# must always pick the lexicographically smallest ID. The heap keeps every
# eligible node globally sorted, whereas restarting `min()` from scratch
# each round would be O(n^2) on wide graphs. Ties are by code point
# (Python str ordering), which the deterministic order relies on.
# Any leftovers are part of a cycle (self-loops and long chains alike).
# We do not try to report the cycle path; SPEC only fixes the code.
# `changes` has no SPEC-sanctioned default: an absent key is as invalid
# as a non-array, because silently planning an empty release from a
# malformed request would report success without doing anything.
# Reverse of the FULL topological order, filtered to applied records.
# Reverse-filter (not reverse after filtering) matters: the relative
# order of applied entries is the reverse of where they sit in the
# complete order, so anything planned later always rolls back first,
# even when intermediate changes were never applied.
# Only not-yet-applied records are emitted. Already applied entries
# already satisfied their dependencies in the graph above, so they do

routines.name: retained_closure
routines.docstring:
Return every applied ID that must survive a rollback, or raise.

G2 rule 3. Two independent reasons to keep an ID, unioned:

- the caller explicitly listed it in `retain`;
- it is an APPLIED transitive dependency of something retained.

"Applied and required by" is the precise reading of the rule: edges point
from a change to what it needs, so we walk forward along `depends_on` from
each retained ID. A dependency in the graph that was never applied needs
no protection -- it is not being rolled back anyway, and it must not be
forced into the output either.

Seeding the walk with the retained set itself (rather than only their
dependencies) is what makes the closure return exactly what the caller
asked for plus its dependencies; the rollback filter then keeps those and
emits the rest. A dependency edge can never lead back into the retained
set, because build_order already proved the graph acyclic, so the walk
terminates on structure alone.

Every walk edge is already known to exist (build_order rejected dangling
targets) and to be acyclic (build_order rejected cycles), so this needs no
cycle handling of its own; the `keep` membership test additionally makes
the work linear in edges for diamond-shaped graphs and shared sub-chains.

unsupported-action: nothing about a frozen release is worth validating
further, and the caller must learn the freeze rather than a detail.

Both spellings of "environment is broken" collapse into invalid-
environment while `production` itself deliberately does not: dropping the
key from ENVIRONMENTS would report invalid-environment, which G2
explicitly forbids ("return the normal error object with production-
frozen").

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Return `(action, budget)` or raise PolicyError.

Assumes check_environment already passed (planner calls it first). Order
is still observable through error codes and is contractual: action ->
budget. Do not reorder; tests pin it.

Budget is a nonnegative integer, booleans excluded (`type(...) is not int`
rather than isinstance, since bool subclasses int).

routines.name: budget_caps
routines.docstring:
Whether `budget` bounds emitted units for this action.

Rollback is a retraction of work already paid for; capping it would make
the system unable to undo a release it just performed, so the budget is
validated but not applied. The field stays required for both actions.

routines.name: effective_budget
routines.docstring:
The budget actually enforced for `action`.

Plan: min(request, STAGING_BUDGET_CAP). Rollback: returned unchanged; the
planner never compares it because budget_caps(action) is false, but the
value is still handed back so the ceiling cannot leak onto rollback by
accident if the caller's guard ever changes.

routines.name: retain_ids
routines.docstring:
Validate `retain` and return it as an ordered, de-duplicated list.

G2 rule 3. `retain` is optional and defaults to an empty list; an explicit
`null` is rejected because, like `depends_on`, only the absent key is
sanctioned as "use the default" -- silently reading null as empty would
let a malformed caller appear to request a full rollback.

Only the SHAPE is judged here. "Already applied" can only be checked
against the journal, which journal.py owns, so applied-ness is enforced in
planner.retained_closure and reported with this same code.

comments: # G2: the release is staging-only, so `production` deliberately maps to NO
# actions. Dropping the key entirely would make `production` report
# invalid-environment, which G2 forbids; keeping the key with an empty tuple
# lets check_environment tell "unknown name" from "known but frozen".
# G2 staging plan budget ceiling. The effective budget is the MINIMUM of the
# caller's request and this value, so a generous request cannot widen it and an
# already-tight request stays tight. Rollback is not capped at all.
# `not in` on an unhashable value (a list arrives straight from JSON) would
# raise TypeError instead of a domain error, so test membership via an
# isinstance guard: only strings can name an environment.
# No supported actions == the release is frozen in that environment.
policy.py.moduleNote:
Validate release policy before computing actions.

Owns: environment, action and budget validation plus the budget contract.
Does NOT own: changes/graph inspection. Must not import planner or journal.

comments: # UnicodeDecodeError is a ValueError subclass, so undecodable stdin
# bytes are reported as invalid-json instead of crashing the process.
# Any request, including domain errors, must exit normally.
# Python's decoder accepts NaN/Infinity, which the JSON grammar does
# not; such a payload must be invalid-json rather than flow onward.
release.py.moduleNote:
JSON transport for the release planner.

Owns transport only: read one JSON value from stdin, hand it to
planner.plan, print exactly one JSON object. The import direction is fixed
(release -> planner); do not add domain rules here.
